title: Narrative Devices
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien responds to a claim that there is absolutely no evidence behind government moves to limit device use in schools. He grants that anecdotes are not evidence, then builds an empirical case from a 2026 classroom study of notification interruptions, split-attention and extraneous load, and the handwriting-versus-typing literature. He adds Paul Kirschner on cognitive outsourcing, arguing that devices let students hand the thinking to a platform, and reports that his own school moved homework to pen and paper because of AI. He concedes that a fixed device time limit is arbitrary and hard to implement and that devices are sometimes necessary. His broader move is to defend limits on classroom devices as evidence-based and to criticise commentators who have left the classroom, have a financial stake, and decline to commit to a position.
points: The claim that there is no evidence for limiting classroom devices is attacked with specific research on notification interruptions (seven seconds of lost processing each) and split attention.
Handwriting forces summarising and builds fine motor and memory links, while typing can become automatic transcription without thought.
Cognitive outsourcing to AI and other devices makes students passive partners, which is why the author moved homework to pen and paper.
The author concedes that arbitrary device time limits are hard to implement and that some subjects and students genuinely need devices.
He questions the motives of commentators with a financial stake in their ideology who no longer teach and hedge rather than take a clear stand.
quotes: But anecdotes are not evidence. They are useful. They are likely to be true (as all of the above examples have been experienced first hand), but they are neither peer reviewed nor an argument I could moor my ship to if somebody chose to challenge the idea of limiting device use in class.

The results of this study showed that for every notification a student received that it interrupted cognitive processing by seven seconds! Now to think about an average student in secondary school and the number of notifications they are likely to receive when they are on a device across various forms of social media, potential school messaging apps and even school communication itself through the learning management system and other teachers chronicle entries.

The challenge with typing, is that as a process it can become automatic for humans and therefore we are able to type quite legible paragraphs and copy statements word for word without any true level of thought. On the other hand, handwriting is tough and slow. We have to make compromises to be able to keep up with the pace of the lesson which leads to active cognitive friction as we must summarise and therefore make meaning of the knowledge in different forms.
Human beings by nature tend to be lazy. Thinking is hard and we’re not good at it, therefore if there is a way to outsource that thinking to another device, it is amazing how many people will.

Even with limited device use in my classes, students will attempt to use AI to solve their problems the moment they get the opportunity. Due to this we have moved to pen and paper homework solely because then even if the students do use AI, they at least have to think about transferring the outsourced thinking to paper afterwards.

I also do not think that devices should be completely cast out, even though I would happily teacher without devices in my class at all if I could. There are obviously some functional needs of students that makes device use a requirement. There are also some tasks or tools which work far better on a device or there is no proxy otherwise.

But to say there is no evidence supporting the limiting of device use in classrooms is absurd. It is attempting to appeal to a crowd which I have no doubt has been burned for a long time by policy churn and the carousel of intervention. I would say to this crowd however, what do you really stand for? Do you stand for learning and student progress?
